text: Time to put the last three lessons together and write one real, complete stored procedure, twice. The task is simple: given a product ID, return that product's list price. We'll build it in T-SQL, then build the exact same thing in PL/SQL, so you can see every real difference side by side instead of in isolation.

Here's the T-SQL version. Create procedure dbo dot get product price, at product id int, at price decimal ten two output, as, begin, select at price equals list price from production dot product where product id equals at product id, end. The shape is create procedure, schema dot name, parameters, as, begin, end. And to get a value back out, you mark the parameter output — right there in the definition.

Calling it: declare at result price decimal ten two, exec dbo dot get product price, at product id equals seven oh seven, at price equals at result price output. See that output keyword again, at the call site this time? That's not optional — and here's the trap: if you forget it here, the statement still runs, no error, it just quietly never fills in at result price. That's a genuinely confusing T-SQL gotcha worth remembering.

Now PL/SQL. Create or replace procedure get product price, p underscore product underscore id, in number, p underscore price, out number, is, begin, select list price into p underscore price from products where product id equals p underscore product id, end. Notice the parameter list itself says in and out — the direction is settled right there when the procedure is created, not left to the caller to remember.

Calling it from an anonymous block: declare v underscore result price number, begin, get product price open paren seven oh seven comma v underscore result price close paren, dbms output put line v underscore result price, end. No output keyword needed anywhere in this call — PL/SQL already knows p underscore price is an out parameter from the definition. And PL/SQL actually gives you a third option T-SQL doesn't have: in out, for a parameter that both receives a value and returns one.

So: T-SQL's output keyword has to be repeated at both ends, and only gives you two real states. PL/SQL's in, out, and in out are declared once and give you three. Next lesson, we do the same exercise for MySQL and PostgreSQL — including a Postgres feature that's newer than you might expect: real stored procedures only arrived in PostgreSQL 11. See you there.
